summary: Describes how to carry traffic from several network protocols over a Frame Relay network, covering both bridged and routed traffic. It also gives a simple method for splitting large frames so they fit over links that accept only smaller ones. It was replaced by RFC 2427.

eli5.summary: Frame Relay is a delivery truck with small cargo bays. This memo says how to label different kinds of packages and cut big ones into pieces so they fit.

subtitle: How routers and bridges wrap IP, OSI and LAN traffic in Frame Relay frames, and how to split big packets to fit.

tldr.problem: A Frame Relay network carries frames over virtual circuits but has no built-in way to say which protocol is inside, so routers and bridges from different vendors could not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: Every frame carries a Q.922 address, a control octet of 0x03 and a Network Level Protocol ID (NLPID). The NLPID either names the protocol directly (0xCC for IP) or announces a SNAP header (0x80) for protocols and bridged LAN frames that have no NLPID.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1490 also defines ARP and Inverse ARP over Frame Relay, a bridging model, and a simple fragmentation scheme. It is a Draft Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 2427.

today: RFC 1490 is a Draft Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2427, so new work should follow that document. It obsoleted RFC 1294.

sections.title: Scope and the Frame Relay Setting
sections.content:
RFC 1490 describes an encapsulation method for carrying network interconnect traffic, both routed and bridged, over a Frame Relay backbone. It applies to end stations (DTEs) on a public or private Frame Relay network. It does not describe the behavior of the network equipment (DCEs) except where a DTE must react.

The network offers virtual circuits, and each one is identified at a Frame Relay interface by a Data Link Connection Identifier (DLCI). In most circumstances DLCIs have only local significance. The rules apply to both switched and permanent virtual circuits.

A system that can use this encapsulation and others must know in advance which virtual circuits carry which one. This encapsulation must only be used on circuits explicitly configured for it.
sections.eli5: Frame Relay gives you private roads between offices, and each road has a number that only makes sense at your end. This memo is about what to write on the packages that travel down those roads.

sections.title: The Frame Format and NLPID
sections.content:
All protocols must be wrapped in a Q.922 Annex A frame. Between the opening and closing flag (0x7E) the frame holds the Q.922 address (two octets by default, with a 10-bit DLCI), a control field, an optional pad octet, the NLPID, the data, and a two-octet frame check sequence.

The control field is 0x03 (UI) unless negotiated otherwise. The pad, if present, is a single octet of 0x00 that aligns the rest of the frame to a two-octet boundary. The NLPID tells the receiver which protocol or encapsulation follows. Its values come from ISO/IEC TR 9577, and 0x00 is invalid under this scheme because it cannot be told apart from a pad.

There is no commonly implemented minimum maximum frame size, but a network must support at least 262 octets. Generally the maximum is 1600 octets or more, so a DTE must let the maximum frame size be configured.
sections.eli5: Every package starts with a short label. One part says which road it goes down, and one part says what kind of thing is inside, like a toy or a book.

sections.title: Routed and Bridged Frames
sections.content:
Two kinds of packets travel in the network: routed and bridged. They look different, so the frame must say which one it is.

For a routed protocol with an assigned NLPID, the NLPID goes straight after the control octet and no pad is allowed. IP uses 0xCC. For ISO protocols the NLPID is also the first octet of the protocol data, so it is not repeated. A protocol with no NLPID is sent with NLPID 0x80, a pad octet, and a SNAP header made of a three-octet OUI and a two-octet PID. With OUI 0x00-00-00, the PID is an Ethertype. All stations must accept both the NLPID and the SNAP form for routed packets.

Bridged frames always use NLPID 0x80 and the 802.1 OUI 0x00-80-C2. The PID says what MAC header follows, such as 802.3/Ethernet, 802.4, 802.5, FDDI or 802.6, and for most of them whether the original LAN FCS is preserved. PID 0x00-0E marks bridge protocol data units (BPDUs). For 802.6 there is only one PID because the CRC-32 presence is shown by the CIB bit in the MAC frame, and the Common PDU header and trailer are carried so the egress bridge can start sending early.
sections.eli5: Some packages already have a standard sticker, like IP. Packages without one get a longer sticker that spells out who made it and what it is. Boxes copied from other networks get a special sticker saying which network they came from.

sections.title: Parameter Negotiation with XID
sections.content:
Stations may support the Exchange Identification (XID) procedure from Appendix III of Q.922. It lets two ends negotiate the maximum frame size N201, the retransmission timer T200, and the maximum number of outstanding information frames K when a circuit starts.

A station can say it will not use acknowledged mode multiple frame operation by giving a window size K of zero. Without XID, the values must be configured by agreement or default to those in section 5.9 of Q.922: N201 of 260 octets, T200 of 1.5 seconds, and K of 3, 7, 32 or 40 depending on link speed.

A station that supports XID must answer an XID frame with an XID response. If the remote maximum frame size is smaller than the local one, the local system lowers its maximum to the remote value before it replies.
sections.eli5: Before two friends start passing notes, they can agree on how big the notes can be and how long to wait for a reply. If they skip that, they use the usual rules.

sections.title: Fragmentation
sections.content:
A Frame Relay network may allow frames as small as 262 octets, so fragmentation and reassembly are recommended but not required. Unlike IP fragmentation, this scheme only works between the DTEs at the edge of the Frame Relay network.

A packet is first encapsulated as usual, leaving out the address and control fields. The large result is cut into pieces, and each piece is sent in a SNAP frame with OUI 0x00-80-C2 and PID 0x00-0D. After the PID comes a two-octet sequence number, then a final bit, 4 reserved bits set to 0, and an 11-bit offset counted in units of 32 bytes. The sequence number goes up for every new message and starts at a random value. The first fragment has offset zero and the final bit is 1 only on the last fragment.

Fragments must be sent in order and not interrupted by other packets for the same circuit. An end station must reassemble at least 2K octets and is advised to support 8K. If a fragment is corrupted or missing, the whole message is dropped and the upper layer handles any retransmission. No reassembly timer is needed because Frame Relay must deliver frames in order.
sections.eli5: If a letter is too big for the mailbox, you cut it into numbered pieces and send them in order. The other side tapes them back together, and if a piece is lost it throws the whole letter away.

sections.title: Address Resolution, IP and Bridging
sections.content:
ARP runs inside a SNAP frame with Ethertype 0x0806. The ARP hardware type for Frame Relay is 15, and the hardware address is the Q.922 address with the C/R, FECN, BECN and DE bits set to zero. Because a DTE has no DLCI of its own, the receiving station fills in the sender hardware address from the frame header. RARP works the same way. Inverse ARP, defined in RFC 1293, asks for a protocol address when the DLCI is already known, which avoids broadcasting.

IP may be sent either with NLPID 0xCC or with SNAP and PID 0x0800. The RFC requires the NLPID form, which is 48 bits shorter and matches IP over X.25. Other protocols use SNAP only if they have no NLPID. CLNP uses 0x81 and is not repeated, while IPX uses SNAP with PID 0x8137.

For bridging, the model is remote MAC bridging from IEEE P802.1g. Bridges in a remote bridge group need a full mesh of virtual circuits. The circuits may be combined into one virtual port (the LAN view), where bridges must learn which DLCI reaches each MAC address, or treated as separate ports (the point-to-point view), which may need an extended spanning tree algorithm.
sections.eli5: Because each office numbers the roads differently, the receiver writes down which road a message came in on. That is how it learns who sent it and how to answer.

fields.name: Sequence number
fields.desc: Two octets, incremented each time a new complete message is fragmented.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Set to 1 on the last fragment and 0 on all others.

fields.name: Offset
fields.desc: Logical offset of this fragment in bytes divided by 32; the first is zero.
